item.title: ‘You Know What Happens if You Don’t Vote’: 7 Takeaways From the G.O.P. Convention
item.description:
Vice President JD Vance was billed as the headliner of the second night of the Republican convention, but President Trump stole the show.

With a hug and a handshake, Mr. Vance exited stage right after his speech as Mr. Trump returned to the place he likes most — center stage — to make his final pitch of the convention to keep Republicans in power.

At one point Mr. Trump asked attendees to raise their right hands and pledge to him that he would vote with their family and friends. Dutifully, they did.

“You know what happens if you don’t vote?” Mr. Trump said. “You go to hell.”

The two-day rally in Dallas came as Mr. Trump’s approval has sagged below 40 percent and Republicans fear losing control of both the House and Senate. Republicans hoped the gathering would help energize a base beleaguered by high prices and the Iran war to turn out in droves. But the two days of red meat tossed from the stage seemed unlikely to satiate independent voters whose support has flagged.

Here are seven takeaways from the convention:

Mr. Vance arrived in Dallas widely considered the front-runner in the 2028 Republican presidential primary. His speech offered some early clues about how he might approach a campaign.

Mr. Vance focused on restoring the primacy of the traditional nuclear American family, a theme he has championed in the administration. He did not mention the war in Iran, an operation he has defended publicly but raised concerns about privately. But he issued a plea for conservatives not to abandon the White House over policy.

“Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater,” he urged.

Mr. Vance speaks in a far more scripted political style than Mr. Trump. He caught fire with the crowd when he snapped back at a protester who interrupted his remarks by waving Palestinian and Mexican flags. “My friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there,” he said.

But he failed to sustain the kind of enthusiasm that Mr. Trump commanded either night. Nor did he win anything beyond perfunctory praise from the president, who quickly ushered him off the stage.

As the balloons fell, it was the president alone, along with a tenor signing. Mr. Trump is not giving up his crown quite yet.

Mr. Trump has called affordability — a top buzzword for Democrats this year — a “hoax.” In his speech on Wednesday night, the president claimed that prices were on their way down. At the same time, he rolled out an audacious plan to address people’s concerns about costs: a huge cash giveaway.

He branded his dubious and detail-free plan to send $5,000 to every American adult a “Trump Dividend.”

But Mr. Trump was virtually the only one talking about it.

A day later, the splashy $1 trillion-plus plan barely made a ripple on the convention stage.

The president’s own son Donald Trump Jr. didn’t so much as mention it.

Neither did the speaker of the House.

Neither did the vice president.

Only Mr. Trump did.

If the president wants the dangled cash to be a major factor in the midterms, the rest of the Republican Party didn’t use the rest of the convention to sell it.

Forget about Nancy Pelosi.

In Dallas, Republicans made clear that the former House speaker has been dethroned from her decades-long position as the party’s favorite political villain.

Speaker after speaker assailed Hasan Piker, the leftist online streamer, and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, for pushing what they described as an extreme and anti-American agenda. Their images, including Mr. Piker’s naked torso, were broadcast on the jumbotron over the stadium. Even Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, who is a frequent target of the right, got less airtime.

At one point, Speaker Mike Johnson outlined the new rogues’ gallery of liberals — “Hasan Piker and Bernie Sanders and AOC and Abdul El-Sayed and Zohran Mamdani” — while casting the rest of the Democratic Party as squishes who would succumb to them.

In their attacks on Mr. Piker and Mr. El-Sayed, several convention speakers embraced anti-Muslim rhetoric, including a promise popular among conservative activists to “ban Shariah law.”

“We must stand and defeat the Islamists,” said Senator Ted Cruz of Texas in his speech.

Republicans know that Mr. Trump is unpopular. They are banking on making Democrats unpopular, too — or at least unappealing and unelectable.

Over and over, speakers cast Democrats as out of the mainstream, frequently calling them socialists, communists and even worse. At times they stretched the truth. Democratic socialists might have won a number of Democratic primary victories since 2024, but no serious figure in the party is promoting communism.

“You guys are going to trigger the commies,” Donald Trump Jr. said at one point, as the crowd chanted “USA! USA! USA!”

Mr. Vance, in the closing of his speech, summed up the message so many had delivered before him over two days: “It’s about the party of common sense beating the party of the crazies.”

Six months ago, when it first emerged that Republicans were likely to pick Dallas for this convention, it was unclear whether Texas would wind up as a top midterm battleground.

It’s clear now.

A parade of speakers — from the president on down — used their precious time onstage to talk about Texas’s razor-close Senate race. They sought to boost Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general (even as Mr. Trump mocked his sartorial choices on back-to-back nights), and tear down James Talarico, the Democratic nominee. On the eve of the convention, Mr. Trump’s super PAC had reserved $10 million in ads to help Mr. Paxton.

“Tala-freako maybe tops the list,” Mr. Vance said of Mr. Trump’s nickname for Mr. Talarico.

But it wasn’t just the Senate race. Republicans gerrymandered the state in 2025 to create as many as five new safely Republican House seats. But Republicans running in several of those seats appeared at the convention, seeking a boost in regions that Mr. Trump won handily.

Mr. Trump has long been known as a master of the television audience. Not this time. An average of 2.5 million people tuned in to watch his Wednesday night speech on Fox News, one of the few major TV networks that aired the remarks in full, according to preliminary figures from Nielsen. That was an average prime-time audience for the network, based on the most recent quarterly statistics, and below the usual viewership for programs at that time.

In other words, no Trump bump.

To be fair, the president’s programming faced some steep competition. The first game of the National Football League season aired at the same time as his speech. The season’s second game was on Thursday during Mr. Vance’s and Mr. Trump’s speeches.

Parties in power traditionally attempt to expand their appeal in midterm elections through targeted outreach to independent voters. That was not the strategy charted by Mr. Trump and his allies in Dallas.

Only a handful of speakers offered any kind of outreach to moderate voters (one of those exceptions was Representative Mike Lawler of New York). Far more focused their remarks on stoking fears of Shariah law, transgender athletes and Democratic candidates who were repeatedly described as communists. Again and again, Mr. Trump begged his supporters to “pretend” that he would be on the ballot — an attempt to get enough of them out to prevent the usual losses for the party in power.

Mr. Trump and his allies are staking their chances on their ability to drive their own voters to the polls. At the top of the list are Trump loyalists who typically skip midterm elections.

Michael M. Grynbaum contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Indelible, Unshakable, but Now Fading: Views From Sept. 11, 2001
item.description:
A QUARTER-CENTURY later, the images remain so immediate and so raw, in the way that a movie you’ve seen many times before can still startle you. Dust-covered and tear-drenched, the photographs from Sept. 11 retain the power to take you back, and aback.

Each of these images tells its own chapter, but together, they form the 9/11 epic. The second plane about to pierce the south tower, confirming that the United States was under attack. The jagged and pulverized ruins of buildings that once symbolized world finance. The man exhausted from running for his life. The stillness of disbelief, conveyed by a tea set suddenly coated in gray. No matter where you were or are, there is an intimacy to these historic images that transcends the passage of time. A timelessness.

A universality. We are all caught between watching and averting our eyes. We are all searching in vain for who and what was lost. We are all just trying to hold it together.

Watching in shock as the towers fell, from a half-mile north of the World Trade Center.

The north tower at the beginning of the end.

Taking refuge, and a breather, in a Lower Manhattan deli after the first tower fell, but before the second collapse.

Later in the day, 7 World Trade Center collapsed.

Fleeing Lower Manhattan on the Brooklyn Bridge.

Word got to President George W. Bush during an event with schoolchildren in Florida.

The view from Brooklyn.

Tending to the wounded before the towers fell.

After the collapse.

An abandoned produce stand, covered in ash and frozen in time.

A woman calling her parents to let them know she was safe.

Sizing up the immeasurable scale of the destruction.

By the afternoon, the scale of the devastation began to become clearer.

A tea set caked in ash as if it were from Pompeii and not an apartment near ground zero.

A search for survivors, the morning after.

The funeral for a Fire Department chaplain who died in the attack.

Family members put up fliers in the hope their loved ones survived.

Smoke still rose from the rubble nearly a week after the attacks.

Saluting a fallen comrade at a funeral after the attacks. Hundreds of emergency responders were killed.

item.title: Trump’s Grand Midterm Convention Finale: ‘I’m a Little Bit Tired of Politics’
item.description:
In 2024, President Trump accepted the Republican presidential nomination by promising to “lead America back to the summit of human achievement and greatness.”

In 2026, he closed out an unusual midterm convention organized in his honor by saying he was a little bored of politics. He seemed more interested in telling supporters to swear on something holy — which seemed to be himself — that they would go out and vote for Republican candidates in November.

“Please raise your right hand,” Mr. Trump instructed a rowdy crowd of thousands inside a Dallas arena on Thursday evening. Many of them complied. “I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States that loves us so much he can’t even breathe that I will go out with my family, my friends, I will do it any way — I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going to try and cheat like hell, like they do.” (Mr. Trump usually frowns on election fraud.)

He added: “I am going to go out, and I’m going to get my friends, my family, and we are going to vote on November 3.”

Speaking for a grand total of nearly two and a half hours over two days in Texas, Mr. Trump made it very clear, onstage and in interviews, that he would be relying on the strength of his political brand to see his party through what appear to be daunting midterm elections. He would not be straying much from his comfort zone to help vulnerable Republicans. In fact, the president said on Thursday evening, he was kind of over this.

“We’re going to have a good time listening to music,” Mr. Trump said, name-checking Christopher Macchio, an opera singer who closed out the evening. “I’m getting a little bit tired of politics now.”

Before taking the stage for the second night in Dallas, Mr. Trump was asked by Laura Ingraham of Fox News whether he intended to campaign harder than he ever had before.

“No,” he replied bluntly. Asked by Ms. Ingraham whether or not he thought his legacy was on the line ahead of the midterm elections — “Isn’t this just as important, Mr. President?” — Mr. Trump seemed almost blasé about the possibility of Republicans losing one or both chambers of Congress. “I’ll block all their bad stuff for two years. It won’t be the same, but I’ll be a blocker, what can I tell you?”

The whole spectacle was a window into the mind-set of Mr. Trump and his advisers, who point to recent history as proof that he is capable of beating long odds through brashness, sheer will and an intense connection with his supporters. That relationship is unmatched in modern politics. During his own speech, Vice President JD Vance, the perceived front-runner for the 2028 Republican nomination, asked the crowd to chant his name because it felt “pretty cool.”

Mr. Trump does not have to make such requests. But instead of focusing his energy on Republicans in difficult races — some of whom skipped the event completely — he directed the focus back to himself while he was in Texas. He pleaded with voters to engage in make-believe, and to “please pretend” that he was the one on the November ballot. That exercise might work against him in competitive races where the war with Iran is unpopular and where voters feel that their worries about the prices of gas and groceries are being ignored.

He put a new twist on an old tactic by offering free money — $5,000 to every American adult — if Republicans keep control of Congress. On his first night in Dallas, he asked voters for patience: The war with Iran, he assured supporters, “will be over very shortly after the election.” All of these promises and pleas amounted to a maximalist, midterm-era version of the “in two weeks” rhetorical tool he relies on when he is under pressure, to vow that something good will happen a few news cycles down the road.

“Food prices and almost every other item are rapidly going down,” Mr. Trump told the crowd on Wednesday. “And by the way, oil will be going down as soon as we win the war with Iran, which is taking place right now. We’ll win it. We’re winning it. We control the Hormuz Strait. I think we should call the Hormuz Strait, we should call it the Trump Strait.”

At moments, Mr. Trump almost seemed to be in conversation with himself about his endorsement style, which, in one crucial race at least, has featured a mix of insults and shrugging. On both nights, he defended the disparaging way he has talked about the appearance and character of Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general running for a Senate seat after Mr. Trump directed primary voters to oust Senator John Cornyn, Republican of Texas. Those voters complied and put an otherwise reliable seat into play.

“I said, ‘I don’t really like the way he looks. I don’t like it,’” Mr. Trump said of Mr. Paxton on Wednesday. “But you know what I do like? He was the greatest attorney general in the history of Texas.”

By Thursday, he was basically saying to hell with it: “You better do me a big, the biggest favor you’ve ever done me,” Mr. Trump told supporters as Mr. Paxton watched from the sidelines and smiled through what was at least his third humiliation ritual of the Texas event. “You’ve got to do this for me. You’ve got to pretend I’m on the ticket.”

Again and again, Mr. Trump turned to other priorities, the most pressing of which seemed to be the crowd size in Dallas. There is a reason that political conventions are not held during the midterms. This expensive, two-day event, designed as a tribute to Mr. Trump, functioned more like a temperature check, and there were moments when interest seemed lukewarm. Rows of seats in the American Airlines Center stayed empty throughout the affair. Endangered Republicans, sensing a brush fire rather than a lit torch brightening the way forward, steered clear.

“No empty seats! Fake news,” Mr. Trump exclaimed on Thursday, spending about three minutes affirming that the busy arena was packed when it wasn’t.

And so it went on in that vein in Texas, with little new except for a promise of free money, a pledge of allegiance gimmick, and a few glimpses of an 80-year-old president pondering a future in which he is not firmly in control.

“I want you to remember me in four or five years when this country’s rocketing,” Mr. Trump said on Wednesday, somewhere near the beginning of a meandering and nearly two-hour speech. “Remember, I’m the one that got it started.”

By the time he was ready to depart Dallas, he didn’t seem too interested in the particulars of the future, the strength of Republican candidates or the validity of his promises. He suggested to his devoted supporters that he might be “standing with you one of these days.” But for now, he just wanted to chill out and listen to music. He sped through the last lines of a speech finale he knows by heart after a decade at the center of national politics.

“I just want to say, we will make America great again,” Mr. Trump said dutifully. “We will make it greater than ever before.”

Then the tenor took the stage. Red, blue, white and gold balloons began to fall from the ceiling. The president swayed to the music, lost in the moment.

item.title: In a Divided Michigan, Both Parties Think They Can Take Total Control
item.description:
In 39 states, one party controls the governorship and legislature, a so-called trifecta that empowers leaders to pursue ambitious policies with minimal headwinds.

Michigan may join them after November, but unlike in other states these midterms, where Democrats have the wind at their back, no one can be sure which party will take total control in Lansing.

With all 148 legislative seats on the Michigan ballot, this year’s statehouse contests and governor’s race feature wild cards that set the state apart. President Trump’s sagging approval ratings and trade war with neighboring Canada are albatrosses for Republicans.

But Democrats have their own millstones. In a change election, Democrats in Michigan’s capital are the incumbents, having controlled virtually every statewide post for eight years. And Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive physician who won the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate, has been running significantly behind other Democrats seeking statewide office this year. Republicans hope he is the Democrats’ albatross.

“Many more people tell me at the door, ‘That crazy dude, I’m voting straight Republican,’ versus, ‘I don’t like Trump, and I’m not voting for Republicans,’” said State Representative Steve Frisbie, a Republican from Battle Creek running for re-election in a critical battleground district.

While Michigan has long attracted outsize attention as a presidential battleground state, it has also become a seesaw on the state level. The state once had an extremely gerrymandered map favoring Republicans, but after a 2018 ballot initiative established an independent mapmaking commission, Democrats stormed back, winning a trifecta in 2022 for the first time in 40 years.

With total control, Democrats enacted gun control laws, cut taxes for low-wage workers and retirees, solidified abortion rights and repealed Republican laws that they said weakened labor unions. Then in 2024, Michigan Republicans, mirroring legislative gains nationally, flipped four House seats and regained the majority, 58 to 52. Mr. Frisbie unseated Jim Haadsma, a three-term Democrat, by 79 votes.

Democrats, meantime, cling to a 20-to-18 edge in the State Senate, making Michigan one of only three states, along with Minnesota and Pennsylvania, with split legislatures.

Now, as Michigan grapples with the cost of living, data centers and falling third-grade reading scores, several swing districts could determine the state’s direction heading into the 2028 presidential election.

State Senator Kevin Hertel, a centrist first-term Democrat, represents several blue-collar and suburban communities hugging Lake St. Clair, northeast of Detroit. Mr. Trump won the district by seven percentage points in 2024; Dr. El-Sayed lost there by 14 points to U.S. Representative Haley Stevens in the August Senate primary.

The Hertels are Democratic royalty in Michigan. Mr. Hertel’s father — for whom retiring Gov. Gretchen Whitmer once worked — was once a House co-speaker. An uncle served in Congress, another in the State Senate. His brother chairs the state party.

Yet in this anything-goes year in Michigan, Mr. Hertel has reined in his ambitions and is focusing on his re-election.

During a tour of his district, Mr. Hertel, 41, promoted his bipartisan credentials. Only eight Democrats voted for his minimum wage bill for tipped workers, which progressives criticized for keeping tipped workers’ base pay below minimum wage.

If that were the case, “I think we would have seen a significant amount of small business, mom-and-pop restaurants close down,” he said while visiting a coffee shop in St. Clair Shores.

Brad Kersten, Chesterfield Township’s supervisor and a former police chief, is among the Republicans to endorse Mr. Hertel. He cited Mr. Hertel’s efforts to reduce sewer overflows and secure money for a new facility to store the township’s public safety patrol boat.

“You go with a proven leader, you go with what is working,” Mr. Kersten said. “It’s a no-brainer.”

Mr. Hertel has a significant financial advantage over his Republican opponent, John Goldwater, an oil and gas entrepreneur and first-time candidate.

A former pastor, Mr. Goldwater, 41, decries “the radical left’s agenda for our country.” He supports a one-year data center moratorium and points out that Mr. Hertel sponsored a bill that offered tax incentives to data center developers.

He also wants to help everyone with a rising cost of living.

“If a flood is coming up upon us, we’re all going to sandbag,” said Mr. Goldwater, a distant cousin of the conservative icon Barry Goldwater.

Mr. Goldwater attended a recent Auto Workers for Trump rally despite torrential rains and tornado warnings. Also on hand was State Representative Jay DeBoyer, who is running for lieutenant governor on the Republican ticket.

“John is just a guy who looks at his children and looks at this community and says there are better options for Michigan,” Mr. DeBoyer said. “Enough is enough of the experiment over the last eight years.”

In the House, critical races are in metro Detroit, Marquette in the Upper Peninsula and Battle Creek, where a Frisbie-Haadsma rematch overlaps with a high-stakes federal contest between the incumbent U.S. representative, Bill Huizenga, a Republican, and State Senator Sean McCann, a Democrat.

Mr. Frisbie, 63, is a retired paramedic and ambulance service administrator who taught at Kellogg Community College. As an elected Calhoun County commissioner, he overlapped with Mr. Haadsma, a 68-year-old labor relations lawyer, for a few years.

Mr. Frisbie sponsored a measure to direct fuel tax money to fix roads and bridges, which was incorporated into an infrastructure package signed by Ms. Whitmer. He supported modernizing Michigan’s fragile dams, but he also voted to repeal clean energy and wetland protections measures.

“I label myself a common-sense conservative,” he said.

To Mr. Haadsma, a Democratic trifecta means prioritizing health care, job creation and public education.

And while Dr. El-Sayed narrowly lost Calhoun County in the primary, Mr. Haadsma says voters are energized.

“If Haley Stevens, at least in this area, had been a candidate, some of those young, passionate voters on the Democratic side would be less likely to come out,” he said.

While giving a tour of Battle Creek’s struggling downtown, Mr. Haadsma was waiting to cross the street when a motorist rolled down his window and shouted, “Hey, I remember you — which one are you?”

“Haadsma — don’t confuse me with Huizenga!” he replied.

“Haadsma!” the driver blurted out. “I think you came to my house one time.”

“You supporting me again this year?”

“I’m kind of on the fence,” the driver said.

item.title: DNA From Cigarette Leads to Arrest in Unsolved Murder
item.description:
The break in the unsolved murder case came from a cigarette butt.

On June 16, the police in Tacoma, Wash., pulled over the driver of a pickup truck in a traffic stop.

During the stop, Edwin Lee Newlander, 59, flicked a cigarette out the window, the authorities said. The police officers picked it up and bagged it.

The filter carried Mr. Newlander’s DNA, and when the Washington State Patrol Crime Laboratory ran it, the profile came back linked to three crimes where DNA had been previously collected: a 2021 killing and two rape cases.

The killing of a Tacoma woman found in a ditch had gone unsolved for nearly five years. Around 7:30 a.m. on Oct. 12, 2021, police officers responded to a report of a woman’s body being found. Witnesses spotted a man near the body who fled in an S.U.V. It was too dark for them to provide the authorities with a description, according to court records.

The woman had died from compression of the neck, according to court documents, which identify her only by the initials K.S. There were a number of “external abrasions and contusions,” according to court documents. Drugs were found in her system.

Fingernail clippings from her left hand held a mixture of DNA. Detectives at the time ran the genetic profile through the Combined DNA Index System, or CODIS, the F.B.I.’s national database program, which allows labs across the U.S. to test genetic profiles electronically. But nothing came back.

What eventually pointed detectives to Mr. Newlander was a rape case years later. That episode occurred in 2025, but during an interview with detectives this May, the victim provided more details. She told them that she had been raped by a man named “Ed.” She also provided them with a physical description of the suspect, a white man in his 50s, who was short, stocky and balding.

On June 9, she was found dead at a gas station in Tacoma, and medical examiners ruled her death an overdose. Surveillance video from the gas station parking lot showed a pickup truck that detectives described as “distinct” parked there within an hour of her death, according to court records.

The description of “Ed,” combined with the DNA evidence from the rape case and cigarette butt, gave detectives a name.

Mr. Newlander has been charged with second-degree murder and is being held on $1 million bail after making his initial court appearance on Tuesday. If convicted, he faces up to life in prison. According to court documents, he remains under investigation in the rape cases.

It is unclear if Mr. Newlander has a lawyer.

item.title: Pickles! (Live From the Minnesota State Fair)
item.description:
Hosted by Rosie GuerinCaira Blackwell and Christine Cyr Clisset

Pickles are a polarizing subject. Some people want a cold, crunchy dill straight from the fridge, while others swear by a sour pickle or a sweet, spicy relish. And if you’ve ever wondered whether you can make better pickles at home, there’s a whole world of canning and fermentation to explore.

In this episode, recorded live at the Minnesota State Fair, Wirecutter kitchen writer Maki Yazawa starts by explaining how Wirecutter’s team tested 47 store-bought pickles, and what they were looking for. Then Mary Bartz, a state fair pickle judge, and last year’s overall canning winner, Teresa Craig, talk about what makes a prizewinning pickle. They discuss how to safely can and ferment pickles at home, and the resources Mary recommends for getting started, including the book So Easy to Preserve. Plus, they tell us some of the most unusual pickled creations they’ve ever encountered.

The Ball Electric Water-Bath Canner

Easy Fermenter Lids

The Wirecutter Show is executive produced by Rosie Guerin and produced by Abigail Keel. Engineering support from Maddy Masiello and Nick Pitman. Episodes are mixed by Catherine Anderson, Efim Shapiro, Rowan Niemisto, Sophia Lanman, and Sonia Herrero. Original music by Dan Powell, Marion Lozano, Elisheba Ittoop, Catherine Anderson, Rowan Niemisto and Diane Wong. Wirecutter’s deputy publisher and general manager is Cliff Levy. Ben Frumin is Wirecutter’s editor-in-chief. Hosted by Rosie Guerin, Caira Blackwell and Christine Cyr Clisset.

item.title: Boy, 15, Drifted for Days on an Overturned Boat Before Rescue
item.description:
For days, a 15-year-old boy clung to an overturned skiff as it bobbed in a remote patch of the vast Bering Sea off Alaska after it had capsized, killing his older brother and a cousin.

When the three failed to return as expected on Sunday to Savoonga, a small village on the northern tip of St. Lawrence Island, the U.S. Coast Guard set a search effort in motion that ended Monday when the teenager was pulled to safety by the crew of a fishing vessel.

The ordeal began Friday morning when the teenager, Derek Parker Aghnaanga, set sail with his older brother, Sidney Kulowiyi, 35, to catch halibut, according to their mother, Vina Kulowiyi. Ms. Kulowiyi declined to comment but referred to a public Facebook post in which she gave a brief account of their journey and rescue.

“He was never afraid the whole time,” she wrote.

The captain of the fishing vessel who rescued them said the brothers were with a cousin. The three were scheduled to return around 3 a.m. Sunday, according to the Coast Guard. When the skiff did not emerge, officials in the family’s village alerted the Alaska State Troopers, said Austin McDaniel, a deputy commissioner of the Alaska Department of Public Safety.

The authorities sent out search teams to canvass the land on Sunday afternoon. However, dense fog and darkness prevented the Coast Guard from sending rescuers out on the water on Sunday. Crews embarked on Monday morning, after conditions had improved.

A crew aboard a Coast Guard HC-130 Hercules aircraft scanned the vast sea for any sign of the teenager. Family members had provided the skiff’s last known location, said Petty Officer Third Class Nathan Bishop of the Coast Guard.

The crew found the lone survivor sitting atop the overturned skiff at about 10:30 a.m., the petty officer said.

Derek was about four miles from St. Lawrence Island, which sits about 164 miles off the coast of mainland Alaska. He had aimlessly drifted in the north Bering Sea, a vast ocean between Alaska and Russia near the North Pole.

The Coast Guard enlisted the crew of the F/V Northwest Explorer, a fishing boat that was collecting samples of fish species as part of a survey sponsored by National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, to assist with the rescue. Its captain, Adam White, said he was told his ship was closest to Derek, even though he was 39 miles away.

It took Mr. White’s crew four hours to reach Derek, following red flares dropped by the Coast Guard’s aircraft. His crew blasted a horn about once every mile, hoping the teenager would hear it and realize help was on the way, Mr. White said.

“It was the longest four hours of my life,” he said in an interview.

Finally, Mr. White and his crew arrived to see Derek, wearing a bright yellow jacket kneeling on the hull of his capsized skiff. The Coast Guard had dropped inflatable rafts, but Derek was too weak to swim to them, Mr. White said.

So the crew of the Northwest Explorer flung a rope to Derek and pulled him aboard. Members of the 13-member crew, which included seven scientists, wrapped warm towels around him, Mr. White said.

The teenager had moderate hypothermia, he said, and the scientists took his temperature periodically.

“I am not sure how anybody else would survive that,” he said.

Mr. White said his crew also recovered the bodies of Derek’s brother and cousin.

It was not clear how the skiff capsized.

Temperatures in the area were in the mid-40s and wind gusts reached about 15 miles an hour over the weekend, which Evan Kutta, a science and operations officer with the National Weather Service in Fairbanks, Alaska, said was normal for this time of year.

The Northwest Explorer docked in Nome, Alaska, on Tuesday morning after sailing for more than 100 miles from the site of the rescue. Mr. White watched as Derek was reunited with his family, locking hands with one of his brothers.

Writing on Facebook, Ms. Kulowiyi described her son as a “survivor,” adding that Derek didn’t eat or drink the entire time he was stranded.

“He lived on prayer,” she said.

Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: On Solemn Ground Near Shanksville, a Tireless Devotion to Flight 93 Heroes
item.description:
Two weeks after Sept. 11, 2001, Roxanne Sullivan left her home outside of Shanksville, Pa., in the pouring rain, trudged down a dirt road and crossed a grassy field.

Staring out at the incinerated clearing where United Airlines Flight 93 had plunged into the earth, killing all 40 passengers and crew members and the four hijackers aboard, and bringing the eyes of the world to her small town, Ms. Sullivan dropped to her knees, closed her eyes and prayed for the victims’ souls. It was the first day she and others were allowed by officials to get up close to the site, which is visible from her home.

More than 9,000 days later, she remains devoted to those souls, working as a volunteer at the Flight 93 National Memorial, a national park.

“I’m here because they fell in my backyard,” she said, peering out at the 17-ton sandstone boulder planted in a meadow that marks the spot where the Boeing 757 crashed. “I have a need in my heart to take care of them.”

Ms. Sullivan is part of a small band of Shanksville residents and National Park Service employees who have spent a large portion of their lives making sure that the memory of those 40 people and their sacrifice remain alive. They give tours, speak to groups, receive families, lay wreaths and more.

All of which is no small responsibility. Despite its remote location, nearly 80 miles southeast of Pittsburgh, the memorial sees an estimated 400,000 visitors a year, according to the National Park Service.

That figure is dwarfed by the more than 13 million who visit Ground Zero annually. But for those who make the effort — the memorial near Shanksville is nearly 10 miles beyond the nearest highway exit, past cornfields, roadside mum sales and honey stands — Ms. Sullivan and others never tire of telling the story.

That is because many may be hearing it for the first time. Roughly 100 million Americans were born after Sept. 11. They may not know that Flight 93, which departed from Newark, N.J., for San Francisco, was the only aircraft of the four that were hijacked that day that never reached its intended target, Washington, D.C.

And they may be unaware that after the hijackers seized control of the plane, many of the passengers, who learned from their loved ones of the Twin Towers attack and realized they were part of the larger plot, banded together to attack the cockpit. And that the hijackers, fearing that the passengers would retake the plane, chose to crash the aircraft in what turned out to be a grassy expanse once mined for coal.

After Congress established a new national park to honor the 40 passengers and crew, the official memorial at the site opened to the public in 2011. Set across 2,000 acres that span the path of the jet before it crashed, the park includes a visitor center and overlook above the crash site, a memorial plaza and a curved path that leads to a marble wall engraved with victims’ names.

A narrow, 93-foot stone cylinder adorned with 40 wind chimes — one per fallen passenger and crew member — stands tall at the memorial’s entrance, completed in 2020.

Adam Shaffer, 44, head of visitor services at the memorial, knows every inch of the grounds, partly because he was there, like Ms. Sullivan, when there was no memorial. And because it is deeply ingrained in his family.

In Shanksville, a community of under 300 people, his father was the chief of Shanksville’s Volunteer Fire Department who responded to the crash, and his mother interviewed hundreds of people for an oral history of Sept. 11. Mr. Shaffer spent his weekends returning home from college to help guide people who came to see the scourged earth. Alongside a group of about 40 volunteers, including Ms. Sullivan, he stood for two hours at a time in that field, telling the story long before an official memorial was built.

The park today “has its roots in the community answering that call all these years ago,” he said.

Mr. Shaffer, who has spent more than two decades steeped in the tragedy and heroism of that day, steps into the empty visitor center every morning before the park opens. There, a news broadcast from Sept. 11 runs on a loop. As part of his job, he gives walking tours that explain the crash and its aftermath.

Like many others, he said he experiences times when the sadness can be too much.

“There’s moments where it creeps in,” Mr. Shaffer said. “There are always moments.”

But he added that the importance of “the story continuing to live” is what eventually prevails.

Ms. Sullivan works her volunteer shift every Thursday, and she is not alone in her dedication.“We have had people who were here on Sept. 11, and are still coming to work in their 70s and in their 80s,” said Stephen Clark, superintendent of the park. “And they have a shift, and I’m here to tell you, unless there’s an ice storm, they’re here.” ”

Before there were shifts, back when the roads around the site were half dirt, Ms. Sullivan collected items that were left on her lawn as a makeshift memorial: flowers, flags, Army boots, a flight attendant’s uniform. Later, she helped the Somerset Historical Center archive more than 30,000 items from similar memorials that popped up around Shanksville.

“How do you handle a jetliner falling in your backyard? You do not,” she said, as a family bowed their heads at the boulder where the plane crashed more than two decades ago. “I want the next generation to remember what we went through.”

“We lived it,” she added. “But it’s your history.”

Hannah Beier contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: For Influencers, Convention Access Was Easy. Selling the Message Was More Complicated.
item.description:
When Lydia Shaffer, the social media influencer who goes by “Conservative Barbie,” walked out of President Trump’s midterm convention on Wednesday night, she knew she had a problem.

She was here in Dallas to spread the message of the Republican Party to the American people. But the dozens of speeches during the first day of the convention described a booming country, and the president, in his keynote address, called the affordability crisis gripping the nation “fake.”

The reality for the hundreds of thousands of people who followed Ms. Shaffer online was different, and she sensed that such a sunny portrait would not be well received.

“Honestly, people are still hurting right now,” said Ms. Shaffer, whose online moniker has been “conservativebarbie2.0” since her first account was banned from TikTok during the pandemic for what she described as anti-conservative bias.

“Normally,” she said, holding a pink selfie stick, “conservatives are really good at naming a problem.”

More than 100 influencers were invited to the midterm convention by members of the Republican National Committee, a committee spokeswoman said. They were given some of the best seats in the arena and special “creator” credentials that granted them access to a list of Republican Party leaders eager to sit for interviews.

They recorded content from special a platform directly across from the stage where the president spoke. They partied after hours at an event hosted by TikTok, where they snacked on miniature cheesecakes and an assortment of cake balls.

“We got great treatment in 2024,” said Xaviaer DuRousseau, who boasts well over a million followers across Instagram and TikTok, referring to the Republican National Convention two years ago. “But this is even better.”

The difficult task facing these dozens of conservative influencers was figuring out how to boost the Republican Party, when the image of prosperity projected from the stage was different from the reality of surging costs.

Bogdan Laurentiu, a conservative content creator with more than 700,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram, said he chose to stay focused on the issue he knew resonated with his audience: immigration.

“I don’t talk about prices,” he said just outside the platform reserved for influencers, which was called the “creator deck.” “There are a few topics I don’t talk about.”

Ms. Shaffer opted for a similar approach. She uploaded a collection of photos that included selfies with other influencers, her “creator lounge” credentials and her purse next to her selfie stick. She also posted a video honoring Charlie Kirk, the conservative online giant who was assassinated exactly one year ago.

She said she hoped the content would capture the excitement she felt being in a room of like-minded people. Maybe that energy, in the absence of specific policies, would help bring together her party, which she worried was increasingly divided, she said.

Conservatives with social-media savvy have been key to the Republican Party’s success over the last decade, helping the G.O.P. build a winning coalition in part by drawing in younger voters.

With the midterm elections less than two months away, the convention was advertised as an effort to drum up support for Republican candidates running in tough races. To keep control of the House and the Senate, the Republican Party will likely have to win back support from young voters, who polls show are increasingly disenchanted with the party.

But the task of boosting the right wing’s online brand has become more difficult as Mr. Trump’s popularity has lagged in polls and the war in Iran, among other issues, has divided some of the G.O.P.’s biggest online names.

That has also complicated the relationship between the influencer class and Republican leaders, especially Mr. Trump, whose access gives them the content that has boosted their careers. Influencers on both sides of the aisle have been paid to endorse candidates, but it is often difficult to discern who or how much because there are no federal regulations requiring disclosure of payments for political support on social media.

The online conservative movement has also yet to fill a void left by the killing of Mr. Kirk, the conservative campus organizer who co-founded Turning Point USA and proved uniquely able to mobilize young Republicans.

The second day of the convention, Thursday, was the anniversary of Mr. Kirk’s killing. Some of Turning Point’s new leaders skipped the convention and instead streamed a live broadcast from Arizona to mark the day.

Andrew Kolvet, a longtime confidant of Mr. Kirk and one of the regular hosts of his talk show since his death, said on X that he had decided to “remember Charlie here, inside his studio and on the campus that he built.” He encouraged “our influencers and our contributors to come here and be a part of remembering Charlie.” He said he did not see the overlapping events as a “major slight.”

A Times-Siena poll in May found that Mr. Trump’s disapproval rating was 76 percent among young voters, a 6 percentage point jump from January and a 10 percentage point increase from about a year prior. More than half of young voters said Trump’s policies have hurt them personally in May, compared to 45 percent in September of the year prior.

Mr. DuRousseau, who was stopped constantly inside the convention arena by gawking fans, said he came hoping to share clips of “anything that is dragging Abdul El-Sayed,” the Democrat running for Senate in Michigan. That proved fruitful, as Dr. El-Sayed and other similarly progressive candidates were popular topics among speakers.

Mr. DuRousseau said he was also looking for footage of Vice President JD Vance because “it’s never too early” to promote the vice president’s possible presidential run in 2028.

Many of the content creators in attendance shared pictures and videos praising the energy at the convention and depicting the arena, which had a sizable crowd but also empty seats, as full. Benny Johnson, a right-wing podcaster, hosted a livestream of Mr. Trump’s speech and shared clips of it on X, racking up thousands of retweets and likes.

An influencer who posts on X under the account name Gunther Eagleman shared an A.I. video of Mr. Trump handing out $5,000 checks after he floated the idea of giving a “Trump Dividend” to every adult American if Republicans keep control of Congress, an idea that would cost more than $1.3 trillion and has been described by some Republicans and Democrats as socialism, a budget-busting gimmick and an attempt to buy votes.

Mr. DuRousseau’s first video from the convention defended the legality of the plan.

Other right-wing influencers were critical on other fronts. Laura Loomer, the far-right activist who is close to Mr. Trump, took to X to condemn those in the party who spoke at the convention for not amplifying anti-Muslim sentiment.

Ms. Shaffer was optimistic that the two-day event would help unify her party, which she said she sees as increasingly divided.

“It’s happening,” she said, sticking out her hand and cupping her palm, as if to take the temperature of the hallway outside the creator deck.

An influencer who amassed a following for his conservative cowboy bona fides walked by. A man wearing a yarmulke decorated with Mr. Kirk’s face stopped for interviews.

“I can just feel it,” she said.

Ken Bensinger and Caroline Soler contributed reporting.

item.title: What Are Kalshi and Polymarket?
item.description:
Kalshi and Polymarket — the two biggest prediction markets — have become cultural phenomena over the past year as they have surged in popularity.

The sites allow users to wager on the outcome of just about anything, from elections to details about Taylor Swift’s wedding to the winner of the reality-TV show “Love Island.” This summer, they helped make the World Cup the largest gambling event ever.

But prediction markets have faced increasing scrutiny over insider trading and manipulation. Some 20 states have attempted to enforce existing anti-gambling laws to ban them, with some success.

Here’s what to know.

The sites allow users to gamble on future events through “event contracts,” in which users place wagers based on a yes or no question.

For example, a current bet on Kalshi asks whether the Federal Reserve will raise rates in September. The total contract’s price adds up to $1. Users can buy as many contracts as they want — as of Wednesday, paying 56 cents to vote in favor of a rate increase. Winners will be given the full $1 per contract paid out from those who lost.

The platforms make money by charging a fee for each bet.

Other investing and betting apps, including Robinhood, FanDuel and DraftKings, have moved into prediction markets, too. And Meta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, dispatched a small team at his company this year to create a smartphone app similar to Polymarket and Kalshi.

While the markets’ bread and butter has long been sports, more people are turning to the platforms to predict world events, reality-TV show endings or even whether congressional salaries will increase.

A loosely coordinated group of traders known as sharps have mastered events contracts like the mention markets, predicting what word or phrase will be said in a political speech.

In the United States, Polymarket largely limits users to wagering on sports. It offers a wider range of markets overseas or to users with a virtual private network to hide their location.

In most parts of the world, yes. It’s trickier in the United States.

About 20 states have tried to bar the prediction markets by enforcing existing state anti-gambling laws, and Minnesota this year became the first state to pass a law to ban them.

But Kalshi, Polymarket and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates the markets at the federal level, have argued that the states have no such power. They contend that the platforms are commodity exchanges that aid “trades” — not gambling sites.

The two sides are battling it out in court. In July, Nevada became the first state to force Kalshi to restrict users from wagering on sports, elections and entertainment. And a state judge in Seattle last month barred Kalshi from most operations in Washington State.

Appeals courts have also weighed in. Late last month, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit in San Francisco ruled that states had the ability to regulate prediction markets. But the ruling contradicted a decision in April by the Third Circuit court in Philadelphia. That court said Kalshi’s sports event contracts were considered financial tools known as swaps under the Commodity Exchange Act, which granted them federal pre-emption from state laws.

Legal experts expect that the Supreme Court will ultimately decide how prediction markets should be regulated.

The huge popularity of Kalshi and Polymarket has created fears about how susceptible they are to manipulation by those with insider information. The sites have rules against using inside information to place wagers, but many users have been caught trying to manipulate the markets anyway.

Kalshi last week banned multiple users for insider trading, including George Santos, the former representative from New York. Mr. Santos faced allegations of insider trading after he placed bets on Kalshi about whether he would attend President Trump’s State of the Union address in February. Before the speech, he posted on social media that he planned to attend but then didn’t.

In July, Kalshi said a White House teleprompter operator had used his position to win around $100,000 betting on what Mr. Trump would say in his speeches.

And in April, an Army Special Forces soldier who helped capture Nicolás Maduro, the president of Venezuela, was charged with using classified information to make more than $400,000 betting on Polymarket on various outcomes related to the mission. The soldier has pleaded not guilty.

Additionally, some lawmakers and others have said they are worried that the sites fuel gambling addictions and prey on users.

The Trump family has built up a financial stake in the industry since last year. The president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., joined Kalshi as an adviser last year and received shares in the company worth more than $300,000 at the time. He also began advising Polymarket and invested in it through 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where he is a partner.

At the same time, President Trump has taken steps to boost the industry. Michael S. Selig, appointed by the president to lead the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, has spoken enthusiastically about the companies and sued states that tried to regulate them. The president declared on Truth Social that prediction markets would “thrive” under his leadership and said Mr. Selig was “respected by all.”

Donald Trump Jr. told The New York Times this year that he invested as a private citizen and held “no policy position and no role within the administration whatsoever.”

Sometimes. Studies have shown that large groups of people make better predictions than individual experts, a phenomenon often called “the wisdom of crowds.”

That means that looking at prediction market data can be useful in forecasting events related to politics, business, foreign affairs or even weather.

Prediction markets are “the most effective way to aggregate information and the crowd wisdom,” Tarek Mansour, who co-founded Kalshi, told The Times. “People don’t lie when money’s involved. You want to be right about your predictions so you don’t lose money.”
